hypotheses.title: Multicall cap check measures Size's own aToken balance, so the borrow aToken cap can be bypassed
hypotheses.description: Deposit.executeDeposit skips validateBorrowATokenCap when state.data.isMulticall is true. It relies on Multicall to enforce the cap afterwards through validateBorrowATokenIncreaseLteDebtTokenDecrease. Multicall measures the supply with state.data.borrowAToken.balanceOf(address(this)), which is only the aTokens held by the Size contract (repaid funds awaiting claim), not borrowAToken.totalSupply(). A user deposit mints to the user, not to Size, so the measured value does not move on deposits. Both borrowATokenSupplyAfter > borrowATokenCap and the 'increase' term then ignore the deposit. The cap check is effectively dead inside a multicall. The isMulticall flag is also reset to false by any nested multicall, but that only makes checks stricter.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) The attacker calls multicall([deposit(borrowToken, hugeAmount, attacker)]). 2) executeDeposit sees isMulticall == true and skips validateBorrowATokenCap. 3) The final check compares Size's own balance before and after, which is unchanged, so it does not revert. 4) totalSupply of the borrow aToken is now far above borrowATokenCap.
hypotheses.impact: The admin-set borrowATokenCap (the main risk limit on protocol exposure to the variable pool) can be exceeded without limit by anyone who wraps deposits in a multicall.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use state.data.borrowAToken.totalSupply() in Multicall for the before and after values, matching what validateBorrowATokenCap checks. Make the isMulticall flag non-reentrant, for example by saving and restoring the previous value.

hypotheses.title: Liquidator reward is computed from futureValue in borrow-token units but added to collateral-token amounts
hypotheses.description: In the profitable branch, `liquidatorReward = min(assignedCollateral - debtInCollateralToken, mulDivUp(debtPosition.futureValue, liquidationRewardPercent, PERCENT))`. `futureValue` is in borrow-token decimals (for example USDC with 6 decimals). `assignedCollateral` and `debtInCollateralToken` are in collateral-token decimals (for example WETH with 18). No price or decimals conversion is applied to the reward term. With USDC debt and WETH collateral the reward is about 1e12 times too small. With equal decimals it ignores the price, so it can be far too large or too small. The `min` with the surplus then hides the error in the large case.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A WETH-collateral, USDC-debt position becomes liquidatable with surplus collateral. 2. A liquidator pays `futureValue` USDC. 3. They receive `debtInCollateralToken` plus a reward of roughly `futureValue * pct` in wei, which is near zero. 4. The surplus stays with the borrower, or goes to the protocol through the `collateralProtocolPercent` split.
hypotheses.impact: Liquidators earn almost no reward, or an arbitrary amount, so liquidations are poorly incentivised or mispriced. Bad debt can build up in volatile markets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the reward in collateral units, for example `mulDivUp(assignedCollateral, liquidationRewardPercent, PERCENT)` or `mulDivUp(debtInCollateralToken, ...)`. Keep the cap against the surplus.

hypotheses.title: validateVariablePoolHasEnoughLiquidity reads the underlying balance of the Aave Pool, which holds none
hypotheses.description: The function computes liquidity as underlyingBorrowToken.balanceOf(address(state.data.variablePool)) and reverts with NOT_ENOUGH_BORROW_ATOKEN_LIQUIDITY if liquidity < amount. On Aave v3, supply() transfers the underlying to the reserve's aToken contract (aTokenAddress), not to the Pool. The Pool contract itself holds essentially no underlying. Size.buyCreditMarket, sellCreditMarket and liquidateWithReplacement all end with this check using a non-zero cash amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) The protocol is deployed against a real Aave v3 Pool. 2) Any user calls buyCreditMarket or sellCreditMarket, or a keeper calls liquidateWithReplacement. 3) After executing, Size calls validateVariablePoolHasEnoughLiquidity(amount), which sees balanceOf(pool) of about 0 and reverts.
hypotheses.impact: All market orders and liquidate-with-replacement revert on a real Aave deployment, so the protocol cannot originate or trade loans. It only works against a mock pool that holds the tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the balance of the reserve's aToken address (getReserveData(asset).aTokenAddress), or the pool's available liquidity as Aave defines it, instead of the Pool address.

hypotheses.title: Deposit credits the contract's entire ETH balance, so stray ETH is credited to the next ETH depositor
hypotheses.description: When `msg.value > 0`, `executeDeposit` ignores the validated `msg.value` and sets `amount = address(this).balance`. That amount is wrapped to WETH and credited to `params.to`. Every Size entry point is payable (`repay`, `withdraw`, `claim` and others), and ETH can also be force-sent. Any ETH left in the contract is therefore credited to whoever makes the next ETH deposit. `validateDeposit` only checks `msg.value == params.amount`, which does not bound the credited amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A user mistakenly sends ETH with `repay{value: x}`, or ETH is force-sent. 2. The attacker calls `deposit{value: 1 wei}` with WETH as the token and `params.to` set to themselves. 3. `amount` becomes `address(this).balance`, including the stray ETH, and the attacker is credited with all of it.
hypotheses.impact: Stray ETH can be captured by the next ETH depositor. Impact is limited to mistaken or forced ETH.
hypotheses.recommendation: Credit exactly `params.amount`, or use a balance delta measured before and after. Make the non-deposit entry points non-payable except where multicall needs it.

hypotheses.title: All withdrawals depend on the price feed, so oracle or sequencer downtime blocks users without debt
hypotheses.description: Size.withdraw always ends with validateUserIsNotBelowOpeningLimitBorrowCR(msg.sender), which calls collateralRatio(). collateralRatio() calls priceFeed.getPrice() before it checks debt != 0. PriceFeed.getPrice() reverts on a stale feed, a down sequencer, or within the 1-hour grace period after the sequencer restarts. A user with no debt, such as a pure lender or a collateral depositor, therefore cannot withdraw during any oracle outage.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) The Chainlink base or quote feed goes stale, or the L2 sequencer restarts. 2) Any user calls withdraw(). 3) getPrice() reverts, so the whole withdrawal reverts, including for accounts with zero debt.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders and users without debt cannot exit while the oracle is unavailable, and a user below the opening CR cannot withdraw at all.
hypotheses.recommendation: In collateralRatio(), return type(uint256).max when debt == 0 before querying the oracle. Skip the opening-CR check in withdraw when the user has no debt.

hypotheses.title: liquidateWithReplacement sends the 'liquidator profit' in borrow tokens to feeRecipient, not the keeper
hypotheses.description: The function returns `liquidatorProfitBorrowToken = futureValue - issuanceValue` under that name. The tokens are transferred with `transferFrom(address(this), feeConfig.feeRecipient, liquidatorProfitBorrowToken)`. The keeper paid the full `futureValue` in `executeLiquidate` and receives none of this spread. Whether this is intended depends on the design, since the name and return value suggest otherwise. If the keeper was meant to receive it, the keeper's economics are wrong.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A keeper calls `liquidateWithReplacement` on an ACTIVE, underwater position. 2. The keeper pays `futureValue` of borrowAToken. 3. Size forwards `issuanceValue` to the new borrower and the remainder to `feeRecipient`. 4. The keeper's borrow-token profit is zero.
hypotheses.impact: The keeper's return differs from what the returned value and its name imply. If the spread was meant for the keeper, it is diverted to the fee recipient.
hypotheses.recommendation: Send `liquidatorProfitBorrowToken` to `msg.sender`, or rename the variable and document that the protocol keeps the spread.

hypotheses.title: Collateral-ratio math assumes 18-decimal collateral and an 18-decimal price feed, but Initialize/UpdateConfig do not enforce it
hypotheses.description: Initialize accepts any collateral token with decimals <= 18 and any price feed whose getPrice() does not revert. collateralRatio() uses raw collateralToken.balanceOf (collateral decimals) times price divided by debtWad (18 decimals), which only works for 18-decimal collateral and a price scaled to 1e18. debtTokenAmountToCollateralTokenAmount() likewise returns a wad amount that is later used as collateral units. UpdateConfig can also swap the priceFeed without checking decimals(). With e.g. an 8-decimal collateral token, or a feed scaled differently from 1e18, every ratio is wrong by orders of magnitude.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) The admin deploys or updates with a collateral token of fewer than 18 decimals or a feed with a different scale. 2) collateralRatio() is far too low, so all borrowers appear underwater. 3) Any liquidator can liquidate healthy positions. In the opposite case, insolvent positions look healthy.
hypotheses.impact: Mass wrongful liquidations or unliquidatable bad debt under a plausible configuration that validation does not reject.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require 18-decimal collateral and priceFeed.decimals() == 18, or normalise collateral amounts to wad in all ratio and conversion functions.

hypotheses.title: Collateral ratio and debt-to-collateral conversion assume 18-decimal collateral although Initialize allows fewer decimals
hypotheses.description: debtTokenAmountToCollateralTokenAmount returns debtWad * 10**priceDecimals / price. This is a wad (18-decimal) amount and is never scaled to the collateral token's decimals. RiskLibrary.collateralRatio uses raw collateralToken.balanceOf(account) * price / debtWad with the same assumption. Initialize.validateInitializeDataParams accepts any collateral token with decimals <= 18. For example, with 8-decimal WBTC collateral, both collateralRatio and the liquidation math (assignedCollateral compared with debtInCollateralToken, and the fragmentation fee in Compensate) are off by 1e10.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) The protocol is deployed with a collateral token below 18 decimals, which the validator allows. 2) collateralRatio reads about 1e10 times too low, so all borrowers look underwater and are liquidatable. Alternatively, the conversions are 1e10 times too large.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong liquidation and opening checks for any non-18-decimal collateral, causing unjust liquidations or an inability to borrow. This is deployment-dependent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Scale collateral amounts to wad using the collateral token's decimals in collateralRatio and in debtTokenAmountToCollateralTokenAmount. Alternatively, reject collateral tokens with decimals != 18 at initialization.

hypotheses.title: Compensate fragmentation fee is capped at the caller's collateral balance and can be avoided
hypotheses.description: When `exiterCreditRemaining > 0`, the fee is `min(fragmentationFee in collateral, collateralToken.balanceOf(msg.sender))`. A borrower whose collateral balance is zero or small pays a reduced fee or none. After the compensation `validateUserIsNotUnderwater` only passes if their remaining debt is zero. A borrower who wipes their debt this way and holds no collateral can therefore fragment the credit position for free. The fee is not charged in any other way.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A borrower with zero collateral holds a large credit position in some loan. 2. The same borrower owes a smaller debt. 3. They call `compensate` for the full debt amount, leaving a remainder on the credit position. 4. `fragmentationFeeInCollateral` is 0 and no fee is paid. The `validateUserIsNotUnderwater` check passes because debt is now zero.
hypotheses.impact: The protocol loses the fragmentation fee, and credit positions can be fragmented at no cost. The effect is small and bounded.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert when the caller cannot pay the full fragmentation fee. Alternatively, charge the fee in borrow tokens from the borrowAToken balance.

hypotheses.title: Mixed ETH and ERC20 deposits cannot be combined in one multicall
hypotheses.description: `msg.value` persists across the delegatecalls inside `multicall`. `validateDeposit` requires `msg.value == params.amount && token == weth` for every deposit call whenever `msg.value != 0`. A multicall that deposits ETH as WETH collateral and also deposits ERC20 borrow tokens, or deposits twice with different amounts, reverts. This blocks the intended single-transaction deposit-and-borrow flow when ETH is used. Because `executeDeposit` consumes the whole balance on the first call, the other deposits cannot be ordered to work around it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User calls `multicall{value: X}([deposit(weth, X, me), deposit(usdc, Y, me)])`. 2. The second `validateDeposit` sees `msg.value != 0` and `Y != X`, so it reverts.
hypotheses.impact: A user experience and liveness limitation. Users must split the actions into separate transactions, which can be inconvenient when time-sensitive.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the ETH value still unspent inside multicall. Only apply the `msg.value` check when the call actually consumes ETH.
